newsitem.title: IRAQ: Iraq fires at U.S. planes, Kurds ready for attack.
newsitem.headline: Iraq fires at U.S. planes, Kurds ready for attack.

text.p: Iraq said it had fired missiles at U.S. planes policing no-fly zones -- but missed -- while a newspaper run by President Saddam Hussein's son called for a holy war against the United States.

In northern Iraq, Kurdish villagers abandoned their homes ahead of an expected incursion by Turkey's military massing on the border and Iraqi Kurdish rebels prepared for more attacks by the combined forces of Iraqi troops and a rival Kurdish faction.

"Iraqi air defence men have confronted the hostile (American) aircraft by firing surface-to-air missiles," Iraqi state television said on Saturday, quoting a defence ministry spokesman. It did not say when the missiles were fired.

"We have no alternative...but to declare Jihad (holy war) and fight them until the last drop in Iraqis' veins...and strongly reject all their means and commandments," declared Babel, the newspaper of Saddam's eldest son Uday, in a front-page editorial.
The United States said it could not confirm that Iraq had fired surface-to-air missiles against U.S. warplanes policing no-fly zones in northern and southern Iraq.
"At this time we have no information to confirm that," said a White House spokesman, Barry Toiv, in Washington. He said U.S. officials were checking out the report.

The Pentagon said 44 cruise missile strikes, mounted in response to Iraq's military assault against Kurdish rebels in the north last weekend, severely damaged Iraqi air defences in the south last Tuesday and Wednesday, destroying or damaging up to 11 of 15 targets.
Foreign ministers of the European Union, meeting in Ireland on Saturday, carefully avoided endorsing the U.S. action.

The government newspaper al-Jumhouriya ridiculed U.S. claims that its missile raids had helped reverse the situation in northern Iraq and the main Kurdish city of Arbil, which the Iraqis captured for a pro-Baghdad Kurdish faction last Saturday.
"Iraq once again proves that it is the decisive force in Iraqi Kurdistan...the liberation of Arbil marks (the beginning) of the great collapse in U.S. plans against it," the daily said.

The Patriotic Union of Kurdistan (PUK), ousted from Arbil last week, said Iraq was moving tanks into a position that would place the Kurdish faction under attack from three fronts around their Sulaimaniya stronghold.
Iraq joined the fighting in northern Iraq on the side of the Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP) to kick the PUK out of Arbil.

Meanwhile Turkey expanded its plans for a buffer zone along its shared border with northern Iraq, with Turkish Foreign Minister Tansu Ciller saying Turkey might clear some Iraqi Kurdish settlements from the narrow zone it wants to create.

Turkey has said the zone, which would be temporary, is needed to prevent infiltration by separatist Turkish Kurdish rebels using bases there for its 12-year-old insurgency in southeast Turkey. The rebellion has cost over 20,000 lives.

Turkish troops have been massing on the border with Iraq in apparent readiness to push against the Kurdistan Workers Party (PKK), but army officials would not comment on reports that troops had already mounted some cross-border attacks.

A foreign ministry official said Ankara wanted to empty some border settlements to ensure civilians were not caught up in fighting and were unable to give refuge or support to the PKK. He did not give any details of the planned operation.
Iraqi Kurdish villagers in the border region were already on the move however.

Scores of refugees evacuated the area around Banek, about 30 km (20 miles) from the main Iraqi border town of Zakho. They shuttled their belongings to a valley further south, leaving behind fruit and vegetable harvests.

Secretary of State Warren Christopher said in London the United States understood Turkey's reasons for establishing a security zone in Iraq and had been assured it would be temporary and involve no permanent troops.
But France, Russia and neighbour Syria have opposed the Turkish plan. Iraq has rejected it as "unacceptable."
